utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue, I'd first like to verify whether the technical facilities are working well. Mr. Stanisic, I can see you. Can you see on your screen the Trial Chamber, or at least me as Presiding Judge? Has the telephone line been tested? Because you have a telephone line which allows you speak with -- to speak with Mr. Knoops. Mr. Knoops, could I ask you whether the line has been tested, and if not, would you please test it right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has not been tested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please test it right away to see if there is any direct communication possible between you and Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, do I understand that you can directly communicate through this telephone line with Mr. Knoops in the courtroom? THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Then of course the fact that I'm verifying that all the technical facilities for Mr. Stanisic are in place doesn't mean that you're not there, Mr. Simatovic, and assisted by counsel. There are a few of procedural matters we have to pay attention to start with, and first I should explain why we had this late start. The late start is due to the fact that it turns out up to this moment to be impossible to have a line with the UNDU and the videolink room in two languages, which means that questions to be put to Dr. Eekhof cannot be put to him through this line. I asked whether Dr. Eekhof would be available to come to the courtroom so that he can answer any questions here, because, Mr. Knoops, I understand that you have some questions for Dr. Eekhof. Yes. May I take that up to the moment that Dr. Eekhof arrives that we can continue with other procedural matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber received the -- first of all, the 30th of November report by Dr. Eekhof, "Health condition of Mr. Stanisic, Jovica," and I do understand that you have further questions for Dr. Eekhof on the basis of this report. Then we'll wait until he's there. Then we also received the non-attendance in court form in which Mr. Stanisic expresses that he feels too unwell to attend court in person, that he does not waive his right to attend court in person, but that he has indicated that he wishes to use the video-conferencing link under the present circumstances, and as is clear to everyone now is that he is actually using the video-conferencing link at this very moment. Until we've heard answers from Dr. Eekhof on any questions that you may have for him, the Chamber also wishes at this moment to proceed with a few procedural matters. I'm addressing you, Mr. Bakrac. The Chamber understands that you would wish to raise an issue perhaps in private session, an issue which relates to disagreements between the Simatovic defence and OLAD. The Chamber is aware of the issue, but the Chamber prefers to raise it only after the first break, for very specific reasons. So therefore the Chamber suggests that we proceed at this moment, but that we pay attention to it later today. I see you are nodding yes, which means that we will proceed as I suggested. There are a few procedural matters which I'll save for tomorrow. There is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The next issue is that the Chamber would like to issue a brief statement on conducting cross-examinations of witnesses. Since the text of this statement has not been distributed yet to the booth, I'll refrain from giving that statement right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to also make a short statement on the agreed facts. The second decision on adjudicated facts is still pending at this moment and will be issued in due course, but I already wanted to address an issue that came to the Chamber's attention in this respect. It relates to the agreed facts, and the Chamber, as it has expressed on previous occasions, cannot comprehend why the parties cannot agree on some basic facts as opposed to simply not opposing that the Chamber takes judicial notice of them. Matters could be expedited immensely if the parties focused on matters that are truly in dispute. For example, will the Defence want to challenge such basic facts as when Mr. Martic was appointed to a certain position? The parties are urged to focus on matters in dispute and try to come to agreements on other matters. In the same vein, the Chamber learned that there may be room for agreement in relation to evidence relating to Witness B-1244. The Chamber expects the parties to intensify their efforts on coming to an agreement on certain facts, including those related to Witness B-1244, and report back on their progress by December the 18th, 2009. I do understand that it will take some time for Dr. Eekhof to arrive. Mr. Knoops, is the matter you would like to raise and the questions you would like to put to Dr. Eekhof, would that be an obstacle to already starting with the first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my questions would not be a problem to be raised if the cross-examination or the examination-in-chief would be limited to 45 minutes, but that not being the case, I expect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say we can proceed for 45 minutes with the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we expect Dr. Eekhof to arrive in approximately half an hour. So that would be a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, I noticed that when we entered the courtroom that you were standing upright. I can imagine that it's not very convenient for you to get up and down again, so the Chamber will not in any way consider it as a lack of respect if you just remain seated when we entered the courtroom. So feel free to do so. Then we'll proceed -- then we'll proceed, and could -- is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, and -- Mr. Groome, we'll have to interrupt when Dr. Eekhof arrives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Edin Hadzovic, and the examination will be conducted by Mr. Klaus Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. No protective measures, Mr. Hoffmann?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: No. And maybe I can raise one issue even before the witness coming in, just to save some time. Would I tender two maps from the court binder of maps. Again those are just road maps and a town map of Doboj for orientation purposes. Those are maps 30 and 31. I think I have indications from the Stanisic Defence at least that there is no objection as in the past. I have yet not heard from Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against admission of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Madam Registrar will soon assign numbers to them. Yes, if you could do it right away, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P80 and Exhibit P81, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P80 and P81 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzovic, before you give evidence the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher will hand out to you the text of the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzovic. Please be seated. Mr. Hadzovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Hoffmann. Mr. Hoffmann is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Hoffmann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, I have just first questions on your prior statements, and I want to ask you if you recall giving a statement to an investigative judge of the Cantonal Court in Zenica in the case against Predrag Kujundzic.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would ask that we could see 65 ter 5172 on the screen. Your Honours, I'm just waiting for the B/C/S version to be shown so he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see now two --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If we could go directly to page 7 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, on the screen before you, you see a document purporting to be a statement given by you on 22nd June 1998, and I will ask you to look at the signature on page 7, whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And is it your own signature, I understand it.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And was this statement at the time given voluntary and free of any pressure?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review the statement before signing it at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And did you also have a chance to review the statement again before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would then ask that 65 ter 5173 be put on the screen, please. It is a statement taken by ICTY investigators on 12 March 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall giving a statement to ICTY investigators on the -- on this day?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if we can please go to the page 10 in the English document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And I will ask you, Witness, if you recognise your own signature on page 10.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And also for this one did you have an opportunity prior to testifying today to review a translation of these two statements in your own language?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And is it correct that you made two little corrections to the ICTY statement, one being on page 7 of the English document. It's the first paragraph. In the B/C/S it's the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: It says in the statement "until 18 May, 1992," and you corrected it to "Until 18 June 1992." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And you made one other correction. That is on page 3, paragraph 5 in both languages where you do mention a number of check-points in Doboj, and the second one being at the Catholic church, and you corrected it that this check-point is actually on the road to Miljkovac and not on the road to Tesanj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And subject to these two corrections to the 2001 statement just made, did your statements that you signed in 1998 and 2001 accurately reflect what you said to the investigative judge, respectively to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked at the time, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution tenders both of these statements from 1998 and 2001, that is 65 ter number 5172 and 5173 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections Stanisic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, numbers to be assigned would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibits P82 and P83, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P28 and P83 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement from 1998, which is now Exhibit P82, in English at paragraph 2 -- at page 2 in the last paragraph and continuing on to page 3, the same in the B/C/S version, you mentioned some of the main activists in Doboj such as Milan Ninkovic, Andrija Bjelosevic and Milan Stankovic. You refer to operation plans and orders received by local Serbs, and I quote "from higher up in Pale or Belgrade" the carrying out of a genocide in Doboj and the plan of annexing it to their Serbian Republic. Can you tell the Court on what basis you made that statement.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Doboj had a majority Muslim population, Bosniak population, accounting for 42 per cent. The Serbs accounted for 37 per cent and Croats counted for some 7 or 8 per cent. As the SDS won the elections in the town of Doboj -- the SDA won the elections in Doboj and said the Serbs did not agree with that, and villages with the majority Serb population started separating from the rest of the area and voicing their desire to be annexed to Republika Srpska. There were all sorts of rallies taking place in Doboj. Karadzic appeared at many of them. They called for separation from the Muslim and Croat peoples. They didn't want to live together with them. They put pressure on the rest of the population, and some of that was tantamount to terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just one clarification. On the transcript it reads at line -- at page 10, first, that the SDS won the elections, and then the next line it says the SDA won the election. Could you just clarify which party did actually win the elections.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: In the town of Doboj, it was the SDA that won the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And what elections are you talking about? At what time period?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first election in 1990. The SDA won the elections. The chief of the municipality was appointed. He was a Muslim. The chief of the police was also a Muslim. All the leading positions should have been taken over by the Muslims. However, that resulted in a dis-balance, and some of the SDS officials turned down the offer to take over some positions. They started boycotting work. They started avoiding any obligations, and basically they did not recognise the results of the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: At this point the Defence raise an objection as to the way the witness is answering the very simple question of my learned colleague Mr. Hoffmann, what is the foundation of this particular line in the statement? Instead of giving the explanation for any such foundation, the witness is giving opinion evidence without giving any foundation for his statement as to quotations like "tantamount to terror," giving percentages of Serbs, and we still do not know any foundation for his explanation of his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, I take it that after this answer you would have sought the factual basis for the answers where it appears that it mixes up to some extent with opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I think to -- to some extent there will be more questions in -- in the same direction. On the other hand, I think he has given some evidence in the statements already. So I try to focus on some of the issues, and I think he did refer to the rallies and other meetings of the Serbs in the region, the attendance of Karadzic and what was said at the time, which is, as I understand, the basis for his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But at the same time, that resulted in a dis-balance and some of the SDS -- I mean, what was the dis-balance. And the SDS turned down the offer. What offer was there? So to the extent the answers are not found in the statement, you are invited to further explore them. But at the same time what is already in the statement doesn't need to be further explored and could be understood by the parties as providing the factual basis for the answers the witness is giving now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just to follow up, Witness, on what the Presiding Judge just said, when you refer to the Serbs did turn down offers, could you explain what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: The SDA won the elections and was given mandate to appoint people to various positions. Since the SDA won, he was he titled to the -- it was entitled to the positions of the president of the municipality, the president of the MUP. Serbs were given other positions and other functions, but they did not want them, and instead of accepting those positions they obstructed the work of all the bodies to which they should have been elected. They simply started creating their own -- I don't know how to put it. Their own bodies. And they called referendums in the villages where the majority Serb population, and that those referendums, those villagers decided that they didn't want to live in Bosnia-Herzegovina but, rather, that they wanted to live in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'll ask that 65 ter 2595 be put on the screen. It's a number of decisions of local communities in the Doboj municipality, all dated 13 October 1991. It's ERN SA02-2842 to SA02-2846.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, did you have a chance to review those decisions prior to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't hear me at this moment in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'll just repeat the question. Did you have a chance to review those decisions prior to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe what decisions are taken by those local communities?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: These are decisions by local communes taken at the meetings of their local assemblies and saying that they didn't want to live in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that they wanted to be separated from Bosnia-Herzegovina and annexed to the former Yugoslavia or, rather, to the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Did you know about those kind of decisions at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can we please go down page 1 to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And, Witness, can you look at the person who signed that first decision. Are you familiar with that person?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His brother and I worked together in the same company. Dragan Dejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if we can go up to the header of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at the header, would you say that this document appears to be authentic to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have a fundamental objection to the document as such, but we question whether the witness is the proper person through which the document could be tendered, because we still do not have any foundation heard in his testimony as far as page 2 of the first statement concerns the last paragraph on which the Prosecution has questioned the witness as an alleged basis for the foundation of his knowledge of his testimony. So in the absence of a clear answer to that foundation question, we oppose the introduction of these documents through this witness unless the Prosecution is able to provide us that foundation through the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any issue in relation to the authenticity of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Not as far as the Defence concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the Defence accept that these decisions then were produced at the time as a result of apparently the bodies which, as the decisions say, issued these decisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We won't contest that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not, then, bar table the decisions which would be -- I mean, in this Tribunal we have a tradition which does not strictly require the introduction of documents through a witness, and of course it there's any authenticity issue, then that should be thoroughly looked at. But if there seems to be not such a matter, then whether it's through this Witness -- I -- it's now on the record that you do not oppose the admission into evidence of these documents, although you put us on notice that you do not consider this witness to be the right person to introduce it. Any objections by the Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to join my learned friend Mr. Knoops's words. There is no point in tendering this document through this witness. He never saw the document before. He does actually know the person who signed it, but he cannot even confirm the authenticity of the signature. This is about the municipality of the Doboj, about one of its local commune, and in principle I agree with the words of my learned friend Mr. Knoops. When it comes to local communes, these are irrelevant decisions. I don't think that they merit any attention whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- now we're mixing up several matters. First of all, whether there's a challenge to the authenticity. It is understood, Mr. Bakrac, that you say that this witness is not a person who could authenticate these documents. At the same time, you share the views of Mr. Knoops who said there is no challenge to the authenticity as such, apart from that it may not be this witness who could give that. And he also said that we not oppose admission of the document into evidence. Therefore, if you say, "I share the views of Mr. Knoops," I take it that there's no objection against it having been admitted, but that you have problems in the way in which it is introduced by the Prosecution, and that a bar table tendering would have been more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it may assist the Prosecution, also for future potential tendering of documents, we have to remind that this witness was from 1975 till 1992 a bookkeeper in Doboj. And really the question is, with all due respect to the witness, a bookkeeper is the capable person as a witness to tender documents with a political connotation like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether a book keeper is excluded from the group of persons who could -- but let's not make matters any more complex than they are already. I do understand that there's no objection against admission, although there's a challenge as to whether this witness would be the appropriate person to -- to confirm the authenticity of these documents. Mr. Hoffmann, you have tendered this document. Do you insist on -- on this witness as the appropriate vehicle to introduce this document, or would you say, well, it gives some support on the testimony of the witness, so irrespective of whether he is the person who could authenticate it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think there is -- there's several points. Of course we can tender those kind of documents from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: That can be done. At the same time, I think the witness did give some evidence on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he said that he knew the person -- he knew the brother of the person who signed it. That's the -- I think the only --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Well, he actually -- if I may. Actually, before I even called up the document, he did say on page 12 that the -- "The Serbs called referendums in the villages where they had a majority Serb population. Those villages decided that they did not want to live in Bosnia-Herzegovina but, rather, wanted to live in Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: It's exactly that context where these decision are in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's save our energy for the next document where there is a real dispute about whether it should or should not be admitted into evidence. This document which consists of five pages, five similar documents, Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P84, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have a similar document which is 65 ter 2596. It's a document from the SDS board in Doboj sent to the SDS Main Board on 16 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at that document, again it's in the same context. Did you know about the decision mentioned in this document at the time, that is, in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That meeting was held in the bank and was attended by Karadzic as well, and it resounded in Doboj. It was a bombshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you just explain what you mean by referring to "it was a bombshell"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: At that time unrest started in Doboj. There was the arming of the army, and the police started separating from the regular police, all sorts of formations starting descending upon Doboj, and we still hoped that everything would come to an end, that the situation would calm down, that there would be no complete separation. However, when this decision was taken, that was the end, and the Serbs no longer wanted to live together with us. That's what the decision meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the person who signed this document, which can be seen on the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: The SDS president. He was a teacher in the Doboj secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And just for the record, can you read out the name, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Ninkovic, an engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same objections to be put on the record, but no fundamental objection against admission as such?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, I see you're nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P85, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P85 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, in your 1998 statement, in English on page 3, second paragraph; B/C/S page 3, paragraph 2, you refer to Doboj being strategically important. Can you explain in what sense you think that Doboj was of strategic importance?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. Witness is not an expert. Also in considering his profession, he is not competent to answer any questions on military strategical issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on how factual the questions are. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I didn't even ask about military context. It's his own statement where he says it's strategically important. I'm just trying to find out what he means by that, and that's just a factual question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think if this is part of his statement and it's not factual in itself, then it's even good to ask the witness about what he meant by that, because then we'll be able to assess whether there's any factual matter underlying what at first sight seems to be an opinion. Yes. So the question then is properly phrased as -- not as in what sense you think that Doboj was a strong of -- strategically important, but what he meant by that. That's what we're seek, and as factual as possible. Could you explain what you meant by it, and try to explain it to us in terms of what you personally observed or you personally heard or what you personally know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doboj, when I look upon it strategically, is an important traffic hub and a railroad hub. In former Yugoslavia, it's the second most important railroad hub, and it links Banja Luka, Belgrade, Zagreb, and all traffic -- almost all traffic went through Doboj. And then there is Mount Ozren, and Doboj is at the foot of that mountain, and Mount Ozren was a centre of the uprising. There were paramilitary units up there, and in the Second World War it was also a well-known refuge of Chetniks and other paramilitary units, so that all traffic that went from or to Banja Luka had to pass through Doboj. And the same applies for traffic going to Serbia and to Krajina. THE PROSECUTOR: I would ask that 65 ter 1744 be put on the screen. It is a newspaper article from 13 February 1992. And if we could please go to the last paragraph in the B/C/S original on the first column of that. And the relevant translation is found on the English page, second last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, Witness, to just read out this one short paragraph that you see enlarged on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: "For this reason serious consideration was given also to the necessity to establish communication geographic links. It is not disputed that Northern Bosnia is a bridge and a natural line between the two Krajinas, the Knin Krajina, the Bosanska Krajina, on the one hand; and Semberija and Serbia proper on the other."

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. This newspaper article referring to a meeting of the SDS, did you hear about such statements at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't hear you well, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I was asking, this is a newspaper article about the --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: -- SDS meeting in Doboj. And I was wondering if you could tell the Court if you heard about such meetings at the time and what you just read out about the links between the Krajinas and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if we can please look at, in the second column, the fourth paragraph. I think it's a bit further down. And in English it's on the page 2, the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: The article does refer to a certain, I quote from the English translation, "Proposal for population transfers."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I formulate an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we -- we first listen to the question and then if there's any need to object to it. And apart from that, I'm not very used that two counsel dealing with the same witness. It's usually focused on one of them. Now, you're both equally fine with me, but two of them is at least unusual. Usually it's one counsel who, as they call it, perhaps a bit inappropriate, take the witness. Now I see that I've got two counsel against one Mr. Hoffmann at the other side. I don't know whether that's usual in your jurisdiction. I don't know whether you have experienced this in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. We were simply fortifying our defences against Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Let's -- let's first -- let's first see whether -- what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to -- can I just raise another issue, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this relates to our client Mr. Stanisic. We notice 45 minutes has gone past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, to what extent 45 minutes will be finally delivered is still a matter to be determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps we remain on the safe side. But perhaps it is good to finish at least that we know whether there is a question and what the objections to that question would be, and then we'll have a break, and hopefully then the doctor will arrive meanwhile. Mr. Hoffmann, what was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, I want to hear from you. You see in front of you that there is mentioning of a proposal for a population transfer, and again it's in the fourth paragraph on the second column in B/C/S. Can you tell the Court if at the time you ever heard about such proposals for a population transfer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the objection is?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The objection is less to the question and more to the manner in which we are proceeding. I would put the objection in this way: That this is a newspaper, from where we do not know. The witness's ability to comment on it, we do not know. We haven't had it disclosed to us as to this witness's ability to comment on this particular newspaper article, and we submit that putting an exhibit in front a witness, reading a helpful aspect of that exhibit in support of a party's case, and then inviting the witness to add a little bit more is an unfair process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's at least leading. That's without any question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Hoffmann, perhaps you could think during the break about rephrasing your question. And not to say that under no circumstances contemporaneous newspaper articles could not be admitted into evidence, but to give it to the witness and then to say, "Is that what you heard?" is -- without any question is one of the most leading ways of putting a question. So therefore if you would consider rephrasing it. But we'll first have a break. Mr. Stanisic, we'll have a break, but I would like to tell you that if at any other moment you feel that you would need a short break, then never hesitate either to address me or to give a call to Mr. Knoops so that we can consider your request, and of course we'll take it very seriously. Most likely after the break we'll -- we'll have Dr. Eekhof with us. Most likely we'll have Dr. Eekhof with us after the break so that we can put further questions to him in relation to his report. May I also invite you, Mr. Stanisic, your last words which do not appear on the transcript. Now wait until I finish what I said, and then -- even if it is to thank me, but there's no need to do that all the time. But that you wait until we finish speaking and that you then tell us what you would like to convey to the Chamber so that it also appears on the transcript. But from what I understand, the previous words were just expressions of gratitude, rather than anything else. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 5 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that Dr. Eekhof has arrived. Could we invite him to enter the courtroom. Before Dr. Eekhof enters the courtroom, is there any party which consider it appropriate to ask Dr. Eekhof to -- to give a solemn declaration, or would we just hear his information?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution sees no need, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No need, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took the last words that you would agree, Mr. Bakrac, although it was not translated to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Eekhof. Please be seated. DR. EEKHOF: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof we received your report of the 30th of November, 2009, and the Stanisic Defence has expressed a wish to put further questions to you in relation to that report. Mr. Knoops, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Dr Eekhof, thank you for joining us today. Sorry that we interrupted your busy schedule. I have a few questions on paragraph 6 of your report today. And in that report you opined that it was your estimation that Mr. Stanisic can resume -- can participate for periods of at least 45 minutes, and you estimate that he can resume participation in the proceedings after a 30-minute break. However, this remains unclear without assessment. Now, my question is, how in your professional view could this time-frame be assessed? And secondly, what should be the frequency of such assessment? DR. EEKHOF: Up to now the problem is, of course, it has never taken place. He hasn't testified up to now. So what I have done, I've looked at the activities and consultations and other things which Mr. Stanisic has done, and I think it has been proven that he can keep his attention and function normal intellectual during at least 45 minutes. That's how I came to the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And as to the time break of 30 minutes, what is the foundation for that time break? DR. EEKHOF: Well, I say that's more or less just an estimation without -- not based on anything but maybe the idea that after half an hour people can come down to rest and clear their mind, but there's no evidence-based reason for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof, is it -- is it your opinion that that assessment should be taken place on a daily basis? Can it, in other words, can it vary from day to day? DR. EEKHOF: Well, the last weeks we haven't seen many variations, so I think an assessment once weekly would be enough. But I've been instructed to write a report every day that Mr. Stanisic will appear in court, so will have every day an assessment, unless instructed otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof, now with respect to the videolink, it is clear that there is medical staff available for consultation in case of a need for reassessment of this time-frame. Mr. Stanisic has expressed his incentive also to come to court. How would you envisage that situation in terms of the assessment of the time-limits and the break? DR. EEKHOF: Well, there are two points on the time-frames. One is what he is physical able to do, and in the last weeks he's been proven able to go to a hospital in another town, that's for about three hours in a car, and with about three-quarters of an hour - that's how I come to the 45 minutes - consultation, and coming back from that town. That's how I came to the three-hour frame. But today I've instructed also the guard to note exactly all his activity on a logbook so that I can assess it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one question for you, Dr. Eekhof. Is my understanding correct that it is that there are no strict medical standards for the assessments and it's rather, to say it very bluntly, that apart from the basic medical assessment, that, apart from that, it's -- that the proof of the pudding is in the eating. DR. EEKHOF: As I said it has to be evaluated during -- but -- in fact, there is no -- I can only do it by observation. I observe and I read the logbooks and see what Mr. Stanisic has done. I also see him during consultations. Sometimes I meet him when he's in the smoking room. So I've got an idea of what he can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. DR. EEKHOF: And what I've put it as a maximum, and the proof the eating of the pudding would be the proof how long he can last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course with -- I'm not saying this but being very cautious about the situation of course. It's not in any way to express a lack of caution. No further questions. Prosecution no further questions. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can ask just a couple of questions and follow up to Mr. Knoops's questions. Dr. Eekhof, on the 1st of September the Chamber issued -- it's the latest of one of its articulations about the way in which we should proceed in trial, and said that we'd have sessions of an hour and 15 minutes. Do I take from your testimony today that it's quite possible that Mr. Stanisic would be able to sit for an hour and 15 minutes, it's just that you haven't been able to assess that because of the types of interaction you've observed? DR. EEKHOF: Physically, my opinion is that he would be able to sit for one hour and 15 minutes. Obvious, of course, psychological span. I can only base it on what I've observed up to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My only other question to you is -- and maybe this is an obvious question. But in your view does Mr. Stanisic have the capacity presently to advise the Chamber or his attorney if he feels that he's experiencing some particular difficulty during the course of a hearing or during the course of a day? DR. EEKHOF: I don't think he'll have any problem with telling people if he's -- if he has a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: One question, Your Honour in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof, the Prosecution just confronted you with a time-frame of one hour and 15 minutes. You just answered, Well, physically it's possible. Psychologically -- DR. EEKHOF: Could be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could. Could be possible. As far as his mental state is concerned, did you verify with your staff, in particular the psychiatrist Dr. Petkovic, whether a time spent of one hour 15 could be endured by Mr. Stanisic mentally? DR. EEKHOF: I'm not confident about that expect because a time spent of one hour and 15 minutes is new for me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So from a mental point of view you cannot confirm that Mr. Stanisic can, in fact, endure a time-frame of one hour 15; is that correct? DR. EEKHOF: Well, I can not also state that he's not able to do it in the moment. It's only what has been proven up to now in consultations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof, since the Bench has no further questions to you, I would like to thank you very much for coming. We'll see whether we can resolve the problem that we can use only one language at distance, if that can be resolved that might save you coming to the courtroom, which is, of course, not very pleasant, not the easiest way of communicating. Thank you very much. DR. EEKHOF: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest to you, Mr. Bakrac that, we would briefly pay attention to the matter you would like to raise at the end of this session which would prolong the next break a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can I maybe raise one other exhibit-related matter before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just again in terms of maybe saving some time, and I just had a quick chance to talk to the Stanisic Defence on it. One of the next exhibits is a collection of photos that I personally took in Doboj in last year just to identify the locations where people were detained. It's 65 ter 5169. It is yet not formally on the 65 ter exhibit list but is pending for admission or amendment to the exhibit list. However, I understand from at least the Stanisic Defence that there is no objection to the admission of that collection of photographs. So I would simply ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: -- whether the Simatovic Defence has any issue about that collection of photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mainly to identify locations rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have not had the time to peruse that collection of photos. If it is not a problem, we would like to look at that collection during the next break, and we will be able to state our views during the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have they been uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: They have been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you know how to use your e-court system, then you can look at them even during the break, but Mr. Hoffmann, you will see when -- at what time you'll introduce them and see then whether the Simatovic Defence has looked at them or not. We'll continue. If you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. If I can ask the court usher to bring back the newspaper article on the screen, which is 65 ter 1744.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And, Witness, can I ask you if you ever heard about any proposal in 1991 or 1992 relating to a transfer of population or exchange of population?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you explain what you learned or heard about such proposals at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Serb -- Serbs asked for those places with a majority Serb population to be separated and that the minority peoples in those places should move out. In practical terms, that was expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Do you know if any such proposals were ever implemented?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Can you explain how, if you know.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as they took over, the SDS I mean, all Muslims and Croats, and I'm talking about Doboj, all Muslims and Croats were fired from their jobs. They started blowing up Muslim and Croat cafe bars and cars. People started moving out spontaneously. Arrests started. We were being put in camps, and we were exchanged. I personally and my family were arrested after the shelling of Doboj, and I was put in a camp. I managed to escape from one of those camps where I was. The others were exchanged. There was a curfew in Doboj. Muslims and Croats were allowed only to walk between 8.00 and 11.00 to go for their supplies. After that we had to stay home. In the meantime, they visited the empty houses, looted and took away everything that was in the houses. They broke in, stole property, and they took us into camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Now, what you just told about these things that happened and having reviewed the article in front of you, would you say that what is said in this article is consistent with what you learned about those proposals at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would tender this newspaper article into evidence. And just for the record, it is from a local newspaper, "Derventski List" and was published on 13 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The article will become Exhibit P86, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P86 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, I want now to draw your attention to your detention in 1992, and especially your detention at the so-called Perco's disco in Vila which is part of Doboj town. And I want to ask if you had a chance prior to coming to court today to review collection of photographs from various locations in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And did you recognise the locations that were on those photographs?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And did you also have a chance to review an index of all those photos?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And can you confirm that this intention that you reviewed is actually correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I notice what Mr. Bakrac said about this photo collection which is 65 ter 5169. Normally I would have intended to simply tender that collection into evidence without going through the process of showing individual photos now to the witness. What I would propose, to give Mr. Bakrac some time, would be to give it a P number, mark it for identification, and then maybe admitted it into evidence after the next session if we have a response by Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want to rely on these photographers with this witness, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it that if there -- they'll be marked for identification then. I do understand that the mere purpose is to identify locations, rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It's basically to identify three detention locations and their exact location in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're now talking about the photos and illustrations. I can now agree for the collection of photos to be admitted into evidence. And this is just to make everybody's life easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that that's also the Stanisic position. Madam Registrar, a serious of photos, 65 ter 5169 receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P87, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P87 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us briefly who was actually detained in the disco, the so-called Perco's disco?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Croats and Muslim were is detained there from neighbouring villages and from the town of Doboj itself. And villages in question were those with predominant Croat and Muslim populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Were these men, women, and children detained at the disco?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Only men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And were these men civilians, police officers, soldiers, if you know?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And were you personally ever given a reason for your arrest and detention?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: In your 2000 -- in your 1998 statement, which is Exhibit P82, you mention a certain Slobodan Karagic, aka Karaga, coming to the military hangars near the Bosanka company. Are you able to tell the Court whether this Slobodan Karagic was a member of the regular Serb police or army?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of a paramilitary unit. I don't know which one. He came to the camp where we were, and he was looking for hidden money, jewellery, gold, and if he found any, that person would be set free. As far as I know, nobody was as a result of such practices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And can you describe the Court, if you remember, how this person was dressed.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: A camouflage military uniform. A camouflage uniform with a red beret that he wore on the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter 4840 be brought on the screen. It's a number of payment lists from the CSB Doboj from the time area -- time period April 1992. And if we could go in the original directly to page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you to look at the list of names that you see there and tell me if you recognise any of the names on the list.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Karagic [realtime transcript read in error "Karadzic"]; Nenad Markocevic, who was a kayak athlete in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Do you know if the second person that you mentioned, Nenad Markocevic, whether he was --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: -- if you know, a member of any police or army unit or any other unit?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of a unit just like Karaga, but I don't know which. They wore uniforms and red berets. And when people were lined up in the form of a human shield, he was on that line where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I just note that a few lines above the name of Slobodan Karagic is actually misspelled, and it says now Karadzic. If that could be directed.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Karagic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If he could then turn to the next page, and I'll ask you again, Witness, if you recognise any of the names on this second part of that list.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If you look at the last four names, any of those are familiar?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Kerkez. He was a guard or, rather, Golub's a deputy in the hangar in Perco's disco club. He was an employee of the Doboj Izvor company, and he was the chief of the cool depot -- cooler depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'll ask that this exhibit be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I put an objection on the record, and the problem is this, that whilst we can accept and don't dispute that this witness has recognised certain names on this list, what we are troubled by is the way in which notice of this evidence is given. What we're told and what we were told in relation to this witness is this -- this is your evidence. These are your statements. And we are obviously given a variety of Rule 66 statements. We're then given, as in this case, a list of payments to a number of named people from the CSB Doboj. What we're not told, what we learn as we sit in court, is the connection between the two. There's nothing in the witness's statement to say he's going to look at this list and confirm that these names appear on the list, and he knows of them. We are, in effect, being made to guess at the connection that this witness is going to be asked to make between his witness statement and exhibits which are disclosed to us, yes, but not disclosed to us in a form which is useful so that we can make the various connections before we hear it in the courtroom. So that's my objection to this general approach to the way in which the Prosecution's case is apparently going to be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have -- when you saw this list, Mr. Jordash, what came to your mind? That is a list of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the list is -- is obvious in the sense that there are named people who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- the Prosecution would say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. But I asked you what came into your mind apart from that you were able to see that this is a list of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That the witness was going to say that he knew one or more of the people on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- so actually, it happened what you thought would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But we were struggling with what's 41 names and not knowing which one the witness was going to say he knew and what they meant to the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I take it that you asked Mr. Hoffmann -- I'm a bit confused about what this is all about. Could you give us further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the problem with that is -- I understand exactly what Your Honour is getting at, but the problem with that is we were, in the first instance, had a list sent to us of exhibits which numbered, I think, in terms of pages, over 300 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So it places us at a real disadvantage to have to go through every single line of those 300 pages, query what might be in the Prosecution's mind, send an e-mail to the Prosecution. One of the exhibits, for example, was Assembly minutes from Republika Srpska Assembly meeting, 168 pages. We had no idea what it was in that that was going to be a part of the Prosecution case, or what it was suppose to prove. We cannot go through, with all due respect, every single line and query each time what it is the Prosecution are trying to say with a particular page and with a particular line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To some extent, Mr. Jordash, I fully understand what you're troubled by, and therefore one of the solutions for this would be -- I mean the witness in his statement talks about Mr. Karagic, and apparently Mr. Hoffmann thinks that this list where the name of Karagic appears is something worthwhile because it corroborates the evidence, et cetera. The easiest way of dealing with these matters is that, and I'm also looking at you Mr. Hoffmann, is to tender it from the bar table, and then in accordance with a very specific procedure, which is accompanied by a joint filing in which you, Mr. Hoffmann, say, What is the relevant portion of that? Give that in advance to the Stanisic Defence so that they can survive. You consider page 8 relevant. We are aware of that now. But for us, page 14 is even more relevant. So please, Chamber, look at page 14 as well. So that we get a focused introduction of lengthy documents. I mean if we are talking about five documents in which it is explained that the SDS has decided that it will follow the wish of the people, et cetera, that's obvious from its beginning. But if we're talking about these lengthy documents, there must be ways to find a solution which would meet some of the concerns, which I fully understand Mr. Jordash, and also assist the Chamber because we are in a similar position if we have to go through 130 pages. Sometimes it's, of course, after the testimony. But if you could give a hand to Mr. Jordash, that will save him a lot of time. It will avoid a lot of problems. So try to find a solution to say any document from which it is not immediately clear two or three days before the witness comes and testifies, it's already look specifically at this page or that page because that's the reason why we introduce these documents. This will certainly save a lot of time in court. It will assist Mr. Jordash in using his time as efficiently as possible, and it doesn't harm you. Would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, and we're glad to follow that guidance. Although I must say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a suggestion at this moment, and it's mainly focusing on documents of greater length. I also want to emphasise that a bit of imagination now and then helps already quite a bit. But 13 pages of names where, apparently, we have only seen now Mr. Karagic and Mr. Markocevic, if you'd say specifically page 9, that would certainly assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the -- our main concern is the names. Obviously we can use our imagination and will with Assembly minutes and so on. We wouldn't expect the Prosecution to indicate each and every paragraph and what it means. We can work it out. But as we understand the case against Mr. Stanisic, the Prosecution are going to disclose and rely upon names linked to various security centres. We need to know, respectfully, who it is they say is connected to the security centres and how those security centres are connected to the Serbian DB. What we're trying to avoid is having names flung into the courtroom linked in some tenuous or some solid way to the security centre and then later on the Prosecution telling us what it all means. And that's why our main concern is the names. Who is it the Prosecution say was working for the DB? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, I spent a bit more time on it than I would usually do, primarily because I would urge the parties to -- to assist each other in identifying exactly what the focus of this case is. If I look only at this document, Mr. Hoffmann, at the top of it, sometimes it says Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sometimes it says CSB Doboj. It's -- it's not -- it's clear that people are supposed to receive advance payment for their salary, but it's -- if you would have said these are the people who are in the camps, that would certainly have assisted, and I don't think that anything would have been lost. So I -- again, and that's something you'll hear for many more weeks if not months, that let's try to focus on what really is in dispute. Please proceed. I took it also that there's no objection against admission into evidence, Mr. Jordash, but this is very short for what was a longer submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P88, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P88 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness if we can now turn to the events on July 12, 1992. In your 1998 statement at page 5, Exhibit P82, you state that members of the Red Berets took out 50 prisoners, including yourself. Can you tell the Court if at the time when you were taken out of the disco any of those Red Berets was referred to by name or nickname.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Red Berets was called Golub by his men; and as he had a Montenegrin accent, we inmates called him the Montenegrin, Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: So Golub and Crnogorac are actually one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And during the actual human shield incident, you state that this Crnogorac killed a certain Kalem. Can you describe how he was dressed? And I'm referring to Crnogorac.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage military uniform with a red beret, and he lined up a human shield. And to give an example of what to do in order to prevent the people from escaping, he shot a bullet into the back of Kalem's head.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Apart from -- apart from the uniform, can you describe Crnogorac?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: He had a large scar from his brow to his chin. It looked like a cut inflicted with a knife. It was on the right -- actually, on the left side of his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: At the time you spent in Doboj and especially in detention, did you ever hear of any other man that was referred to or known by the nickname of Crnogorac other than the one you saw on 12 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if we can please see the next exhibit, which is 65 ter 5012 on the screen. It is in fact another payment list, this one being undated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And, Witness, I would ask you if you can read in the B/C/S original, if you can, the header of that document or the list.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: "The group of Crnogorac," if I can see it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if you look at that list of names, do you recognise any of those names?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: I only know Nenad Kujundzic. He's Predo Kujundzic's brother. Predo was the leader of the so-called Predo's Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to this Nenad Kujundzic on this list?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: He was killed in Doboj. That's what I learned after the war, that he was killed in Doboj and that a shell fired by the BiH Army killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I tender this payment list as well into evidence, that is 65 ter 5012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P89, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P89 is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We did object to this prior to the hearing, and we do maintain an objection. We don't know -- perhaps I'm missing it, but we don't know from where it derives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, could you give any ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution received this document from the RS MUP in a response to an official request for assistant -- assistance, that was RFA 649, a request for any evidence on the unit of the Red Berets in the possession of the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Simatovic Defence has an objection to the authenticity of this document. If you look at it, you will see, that is, if you look at the first ten signatures, you will see that it is -- that they are all by one and the same person. It's the same signature. And there is no date, no visible date, indicating when this document was drafted. We can only tell that this is the year 2008. The document isn't dated, and you don't have to be a graphologist to tell that the first ten signatures are exactly alike. They always read Nedeljko Kovac, and the only very last signature Kujundzic is authentic. And the Simatovic Defence challenges the authenticity of the document and opposes it being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two questions, Mr. Hoffmann. The first, 2008 we find fax headers. 1st of September, 2008; 2nd of September, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Those are obviously fax numbers, which I honestly assume that those are from the RS MUP. We have gotten this document in that form with those fax numbers from the authorities in the RS MUP. So our clear understanding is that this doesn't refer to the time-frame for 2008 but while the RS MUP authorities collected evidence to respond to the official request for assistance that this document was provided internally and then provided to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac the second matter, you say, it's not authentic because they're all the same signatures. Now, if I would intend to make a forgery, I would not put seven signatures all slightly different. So whether this is really a sign of a lack of authenticity or whether it's just person A signing for receiving money which was intended for someone else is -- I do not see exactly yet what the authenticity issue is, because that there are the same names, Nedeljko Kovac, several times. That is clear. I think there could hardly be any dispute about that. But would that deprive the document of its authenticity, or would it even emphasise the authenticity? Do you agree that if I would like to make a forgery, I wouldn't do it this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that what my learned friend from the Office of the Prosecution is true, but before the Defence agrees with the possible admission of this document be shown the request and the reply of the RS. We can only see the date of the fax, but the document itself is not dated. It reads: "The group of Crnogorac." To us this document seems not authentic. All the persons from number 1 through number 10 -- or, rather, for all those persons, one and the same person signed. So if the document should be authentic, it would be logical for it to bear the signatures of the persons mentioned by name here to the right of the all the amount. So I still oppose the admission of this document, and I ask for the request sent to the RS and their reply to be shown to the Defence so that we can see when and from whom it was received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that the document will be marked for identification, that there will be further communication between you, Mr. Bakrac, and you, Mr. Hoffmann, so that you can see the request for assistance and that Mr. Hoffmann can inform you about the follow-up given to that and that the Chamber will meanwhile consider whether with or without that information the Chamber could decide on admission or not, and hopefully the matter can be resolved by tomorrow. Madam Registrar, I think you assigned already a number, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will now become Exhibit P89 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And just for the record I think even the response from the RS MUP itself is an exhibit and now I'll make sure that we get that information to all Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And of course -- and of course the same for the RFA itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: May I remind the Court that the 45 minutes have passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, we've been now a little bit over 45 minutes. I had on my mind to continue for approximately another 10 to 15 minutes and then to have a bit of a longer break. Is that something that you could cope with as far as your attention is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot -- the interpreter cannot hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, one second. The interpreters cannot hear you. I don't know what is it, whether it's a technical problem, or whether it's just the volume of speech, but let's just wait for a second so that everything you tell us is properly translated. THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I first want to seek information that the interpreters can also hear you, and I'm -- if you could just say a few words now so that we first verify whether your voice is heard. Could you just say a few words. THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] I can hear you well, and I can hear the interpreters well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I now hear perhaps through the English booth whether the interpreters can hear Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter confirms that he can hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you then please repeat what you just said, Mr. Stanisic, in response to my suggestion that we would go on for another, I think I said, 10 to 15 minutes and then have a bit of a longer break. Would that be possible for you? THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Yes, but I have a remark which was not put forward today. Over for the last seven month -- months I practically spent in bed, and it is difficult for me to be present even through videolink. It was my wish to come to the courtroom today and tell you in person and ask you to follow the trial through videolink. So I would like to use this opportunity to make that request, because it is very difficult for me to follow the proceedings. But do continue, and I will do my best to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber has considered your right to be present at trial, Mr. Stanisic. We have received medical reports of what doctors say you would be able to do. And as you may be aware, the Chamber has facilitated, of course first of all, your presence in court, which goes without saying, but that if you'd prefer to follow the proceedings through videolink the Chamber has done everything to make that possible for you. So therefore, the facts that we accepted that you would be in the UNDU and not physically present in this courtroom may already be made clear to you that if -- if this is the way in which you want to follow the proceedings and to be able to participate in that, that the Chamber has accepted that choice. So we go on for another 10 to 15 minutes and then we'll have a break, a break which will be a little bit longer because we'll first deal with a procedural matter, but your presence is not required for that. Mr. Hoffmann, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Coming back to the 12 July 1992, did you have a chance prior to your testimony to review a sketch drawn by someone else that shows the route taken from the disco to the area where you were used as human shields?
