utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And was that sketch an accurate depiction of the route from the disco to the front line?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document - it's 65 ter 3566 - into evidence. Again, I appreciate an indication already from the Stanisic Defence earlier on that there is no objection to the admission, so I would not even waste more time to call it on the screen. I would look at Mr. Bakrac now if there is any objection to the sketch being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, the marked map would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P90, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P90 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And a similar issue arises for the next 65 ter Exhibit, 4872. It is a video of the actual exhumation process, and again from the Stanisic Defence I understand there is no objection to the admission of this document. I could have a few questions to the witness about it, but I would not intend to play this video. It's simply a video recording of the exhumation process in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stanisic Defence no objections either?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If you prefer I ask two or three questions without playing the video, and just for the record that he confirms the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I have not seen the video, so I don't know exactly what we could ask the witness what could not be seen on the video. That's -- I suggest the following: That -- that you give us an opportunity to look at it and that we'll then invite you or not invite you to put any further questions to the witness in relation to this, but that is one of the disadvantages of this system, that we haven't seen it, so I do not know how useful it is or how -- or whether it's totally useless to play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If you prefer we could play a very short clip from the beginning that shows just basically the location where it happened, and I think it's important then to ask the witness whether that is the -- the location of the incident on 12 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would that take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I think we can play less than a minute from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less then a minute. Let's do that so that we know approximately what we're talking about. Is it with text or without?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: It's without.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, did you have a chance prior to your testimony to review this video recording of the exhumation process in 1998 in Doboj -- or near Doboj, to be precise?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Does that video show the exhumation that actually took place at the location where you were used as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Were you present during that exhumation process at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I showed them the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that -- those would be the basic questions I would have for the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The video could then receive a -- an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P91, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P91 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And just for the record, the video ERN was V000-7608. The next exhibit I want to put to the witness is a list of names of victims. It has ERN 0672-7955.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And, Witness, once it appears in court, I ask you, did you have a chance to review that list prior to coming to court? And did you mark it in the first column --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: -- did you mark in the first column any person, any name that you personally know?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And in the second column, any person that you are certain that he was detained at the Perco's disco with you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And finally in the last column, one person that had also been previously detained at the military hangars?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If we look at the number 11 on the list. Jasmin Makarevic. Is that the same person that you know and that is mentioned in your earlier statement, the 1998 statement?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: No. Jasmin Makarevic, the one whom I mentioned, is still alive. He resides in Germany. The difference is in the name of the father. This is Hasib Mehmedalija, and this person here is the son of Safet. The difference lies in the father's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And just for a clear record, is it your testimony that then actually two persons with the name Jasmin Makarevic were in prison at the disco?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And did you add in handwriting the nickname of Salih Makarevic, number 13 on this list?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And if we can go down to the bottom of the document. Do you recognise your signature as of today under that list?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this list of victims from Doboj as marked by the witness into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P92, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed. I would say that your next question should be, within the next four or five minutes, should then be concluded if there's anything you could deal with in four to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: In your 2001 statement, Exhibit P83, you mentioned the pre-war ethnical distribution in Doboj. It's in page 2. Can you tell the Court if you know what the distribution of the ethnic groups was after the war.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: How are things now? Or are you asking me about how things were before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: No, after the war.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: After the war, 8 per cent Muslims, 2 to 3 per cent Croats, and the rest about 80 to 90 per cent are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: In light of what you said about the next break, I would rather now go for the break, but maybe -- I understand from the earlier objections about the lengthy documents, obviously, I can't give too much notice now, but at least over the break would I tell the next Exhibit which is 65 ter 1336. It's an RS Assembly minutes paper that I'm interested in one part which is on the B/C/S page 81 and in English it's page 110. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope that it will assist the Defence. Mr. Stanisic, we'll deal with a matter which I would say doesn't affect you in any way, a procedural matter, so I suggest that you take already your break and that we would resume at 20 minutes to 6.00, which is 35 minutes from now. Mr. Knoops, I take it that this has your consent, that -- Then Mr. Bakrac, did I understand that you wanted to go into private session for the the issue you wanted to raise, or is it ... Perhaps you first, but then in private session, explain why the matter has to be raised in private session. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I would give you an opportunity, Mr. Bakrac, to raise the matter, I would just tell you what the Chamber is informed about. Let me ... The Chamber was copied on a letter which you have sent to OLAD in which you express your disagreements with the decision taken on remuneration and -- and clarity, as on what basis such a decision is taken. In that letter, you have emphasised that you would have expected that it was announced that you would already receive a decision not only late last week but at earlier stage you said, and it was more or less promised to you. And further, now having received this decision, that -- that you are unhappy with the decision, with the outcome, and that you give the reasons why. Now, the first question which arises, apart from that this Chamber, if it can offer good services to resolve any problem, it will certainly seriously consider whether it is in a position to do so, yes or no, but the normal remedy you would find in the directive on the assignment of counsel, because we find ourselves in a situation where there's a very delicate and sensitive balance between the authority -- and I suddenly become aware that the witness is still with us. There's no reason whatsoever to keep him here when we are discussing procedural matters. Therefore, if you'd rather have a cup of tea or coffee than to listen to our procedural matters, Madam Usher will show you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, so the first question which arises is whether under the specific rules, you'll find in Article 31 of the directive on the assignment of counsel, whether for, as Article 31 says, for settlement of disputes over payments, whether it is appropriate at this moment to address the Chamber or whether it would be more appropriate to seek the remedy, taking it that we're talking about more than 5.000 Euros, the remedy being that your final request for review with the Registrar, who then shall refer the matter to the President for his determination. And that the President under those circumstances shall request submissions from the aggrieved party and the respondent. So I wonder whether we should at this moment hear your submissions or not. Also, in view of the case law, the case law which emphasises against the delicate -- the delicacy of this matter, that is, that a Trial Chamber cannot assume any powers which are specifically put in the hands of the President; and the delicacy on the other hand is that the Trial Chamber, whether now immediately or during the follow-up of this proceedings is, of course, responsible for ensuring that Mr. Simatovic receives a fair trial. So therefore, the first question I'd like to put is whether this is already the time for the Chamber to be seized of such complaints. And the second issue I would like to add to that is that the Chamber inquired whether the responsible Registrar official, (redacted) is present, and it turns out that she's absent today, so if you would consider that it would be appropriate to raise the matter, which is certainly not clear if you look at the relevant articles, that at least that we should then hear from both parties, but the Chamber would still have to consider whether it is at all in a position to hear such a complaint before the matter has been raised with the -- by a request for review. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I completely agree with you. However, you have to understand the delicate matter and the delicate nature of the situation. We're very happy. The Simatovic Defence team is happy with the way the Trial Chamber understands our situation with the sequence of witnesses, breaks, and the possibility given to us to prepare together with Mr. Simatovic for his defence. Why do I believe that this is the right moment for me to address this matter? On the 11th of September my learned friend Mr. Petrovic and I raised the issue, and between then and the 30th of November we did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the Chamber is not yet convinced that it is for the Chamber at this moment to be seized of the matter, but if you would like to put on the record just to inform the Chamber of what's going on, what the issue is, and if you would then in view of the existing regulations and the case law as it was developed, especially by the Appeals Chamber, then would seek the appropriate remedy, then the Chamber would allow you in three to five minutes to explain what your problem is, but this is not an acceptance of the Chamber being seized of any matter at this moment in this respect, but the Chamber will for the time being understand this as purely informative as you telling the Chamber that you have a problem with OLAD which you'll try to resolve in accordance with the applicable rules and the case law as developed by the Appeals Chamber. You have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed one minute more to tell you why the issues are related and why we are addressing you. This Defence team has continued this trial after nearly three months from a hotel room and with one laptop, because for the time being we don't have enough money, and this impacts the efficiency of our work in the courtroom and our obligation to present our client in a professional manner. For two and a half months we did not receive any information from the Registry about the funds available to us. Why are we addressing you? Of course we have already approached the Registry with the request to review their decision, but we are duty-bound to tell this Trial Chamber that because of the problems we have the Registry, we have a lot of problems putting together our defence and representing the interests of our client and his right to a fair trial. Thank you very much. We fully hope that you will show understanding for us and that you will assist us in any way possible in dealing with our problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One thing is for certain, Mr. Bakrac, there is a dispute between the Simatovic Defence and the level of remuneration that what has become clear to us while receiving a copy of your letter. To the extent the Chamber, without going beyond what its competence is at this moment and can assist in resolving it, of course, we'll give it our best efforts. At the same time, the Chamber will not go beyond what is clearly in the rules and what is clearly in the case law. We have to observe that, because otherwise we're creating more problems than there are already at this very moment. It's at least clear. It's on the public record at this moment, and if there will be any follow-up which would focus on fair trial issues, of course it may well be that the Chamber, depending on what will be argued, may find the matter at a certain moment, I'm not saying now, within the boundaries of its competence, but that depends also on the way how it's presented, how it's introduced. We leave it for the time being in this way, but the Chamber is fully aware that this is not the end of the story. That's -- that may be clear to everyone in this courtroom. Any other procedural matter to be raised at this moment? If not, we'll have a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 6.00. And could the UNDU be informed that the presence of Mr. Stanisic is not required any earlier than ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I see that Mr. Stanisic has arrived but not yet has put on his earphones, we'll wait for a second. Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Hoffmann, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just verify. Mr. Stanisic, you've got on your earphones now, and you can hear us in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And having given further considerations to the time that we spend in court and the objections earlier on to the lengthy document, I will actually skip the next exhibit and move on to one last subject with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Court what happened to your wife and two kids when you were imprisoned by the Serb forces in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: My wife and two children and my mother-in-law were exchanged at Slavonski Brod on the 4th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If I can ask that we see 65 ter 3609 on the screen. It is an exchange -- a list of people exchanged on 4 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you want to establish that the witness was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: It's actually in relation to his family members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean his family members, yes. Is there any dispute about this? The family members of the witness being exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Then I would cut it short and ask that this exhibit be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that there is no, then, objection against it being bar tabled? I see two times nodding no. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P93, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P93 is admitted into evidence, and as we understand, is a document which corroborates the testimony of the witness that his family members were exchanged. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And maybe just for the record, indeed his family members are listed as number 62 until 65, that is, his mother-in-law and his wife and two kids.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And, Witness, I would like to ask you whether you would say that your wife and your children left Doboj in September 1992 on their own free will.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: In the situation that we had both lost our jobs and there was a curfew in Doboj, that was we were only allowed to move about three hours a day, and we had no source of income, and she registered with the Red Cross for leaving Doboj. When she was leaving Doboj, she was only allowed to take two plastic bags -- or, rather, a larger bag with some laundry, whereas the money and the jewellery she had on her was taken away from her and she was put on a bus. Whether that is voluntary, if it can be called voluntary transportation, I don't know. Voluntary transfer, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution will play a short clip from Prosecution Exhibit 65 ter 3536, the video ERN being V000-0406A, and the clip runs from minute 54, 5 seconds; to 58 minutes, 45, of the original tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Witness, did you recognise this man, Jozo Mandic, from Doboj, shown on this footage?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And have you seen his name on the list of prisoner -- of people exchanged that we just saw, which was Exhibit P93?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: And would you say that his account that we just heard about the events in Doboj is consistent with your own experience and knowledge of the time-frame in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We do object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My learned friend's just effectively introduced a second witness as a corroborative witness to this witness's account without going through the usual procedural safeguards which ensure that the Defence are put on notice and proper notice of the Prosecution case. That's our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Our objection goes along -- is along the same lines as my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, apart from that, if I remember well I gave rather precise guidance on how to deal with videos with text on it, that is transcript being provided to the booth and that we would have, therefore -- on the record we would have English and we would have French so that we would have a complete record, whereas now what we have is we can try to find the video again and then read at the bottom what apparently was said. I didn't check the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If I may on that point, we actually did provide the booth with the transcript. And when the video started I did actually expect to hear it, but then didn't want to interrupt. I'm sorry for that; maybe I should have interrupted. But we did provide as in the past the necessary transcripts to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently the -- you did provide the transcript also in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: My understanding is yes. Yes, both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then apparently we have not developed yet a routine which I had on my mind which ensures that we have a complete transcript in English and in French, but perhaps Mr. Jordash is quite happy with it, because that means that the second witness is not on the record yet. Could you please respond to that part of the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'm honestly, at least as far as there is an objection to notice of the Prosecution case, I'm not quite sure if I understand that, because I think we have clearly given notice of the Prosecution case, and this is just part of the evidence to -- to underlie the Prosecution case, and it's part of the Prosecution case that people were deported from -- from Doboj, and this is related to it. In terms of -- that we see on the video somebody else than the current witness to state the events, it's basically -- and I think to some extent the jurisprudence of the case law here does allow for that. It is a contemporaneous document taken at the time of the events. We don't have the chance that we have any record of this witness or his family members at the time. This man that is seen on the video gives on the day of the exchange a clear record of what he went through and how he was exchanged. This witness's family members were exchanged on the very same day. He went through the same events. In that circumstance, I think it's proper to leave that evidence -- or to admit that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, two questions. The first: What did you exactly mean by "without giving notice"? And the second is, would this witness have qualified for 92 bis, apart from the attestations?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Firstly, without giving notice, we have been -- had this exhibit disclosed to us. We did know what was on the video. We didn't know that the Prosecution would be seeking to rely upon the truth of what the witness in the video has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would you have expected, the colour of the buses or -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The fact that there was a victim. What instead the Prosecution will do -- what they've done is introduced Arkan in Doboj. The witness hasn't mentioned him. My learned friend will seek to rely upon that evidence in addition to what this witness has already said about the perpetrator groups, which leads me to the answer on the issue of the 92 bis. Respectfully, probably not. It would not be admissible for this reason: That it goes to the acts and conduct of the accused insofar as the indictment and the -- sorry, not the indictment but the Prosecution's opening has indicated that they say Mr. Stanisic was in control, command and control, of Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Arkan issue, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I clearly have no objection if we redact that little notice. In my view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if Arkan is taken out does the objection stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To this particular video the objection would not stand, but although the procedure -- we would intend to object in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Mr. Hoffmann is put on notice on that. I suggest the following solution: We take advantage of the fact that we had no routine yet. Therefore, we do not find on the record at this moment the exact words spoken. You provide and you tender in relation to this document a transcript in English and translation in B/C/S, and you redact the transcript in relation to Arkan. I'm looking at you, Mr. Jordash. Would that, for the time being, resolve your problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you shared the objections by Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was just going to provide the same explanation, but the matter is resolved now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with your agreement as well. Mr. -- so we -- for the time being the video receives a number, but will be marked for identification and we wait for uploading of the transcript. Perhaps it is uploaded already in two languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: The transcript has been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: It's just now a matter of redacting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, redacting. Of course, we wait until we have received the redaction. Please show it to Mr. Jordash before you report to the Court that you have uploaded it. Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P94 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that will finally cover both video and transcripts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hoffmann. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzovic, you will be cross examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. You've indicated --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You've indicated in your statement of the 12th of March, 2001, that there was a huge military garrison in Doboj in a place called Miljkovac.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in addition to that, am I correct that there was also warehouses in Potocani, which is in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And can you confirm that there was JNA warehouses also in the south suburb of Usora? U-s-o-r-a.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: There were warehouses at the village of Sevarlije and the village of Potocani, which is close to Doboj. There was a barracks where conscripts would do their military service, and there was a small facility in the south, and there were also warehouses at Usora where we were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This was for the JNA, prior to the war, an important military strategic area. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Milovan Stankovic was, prior to the war, the deputy commander of the military garrison in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The commander during -- before the war was a Muslim called Cazim Hadzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's probably not that important, but what is perhaps more important is that when the war broke out, Milovan Stankovic took over as the commander of the garrison?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And all the equipment and vehicles, armory, and so on, came under his command?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you must have observed, I suggest, that Stankovic was in command of the JNA who remained in Doboj. Is that correct, from what you observed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Miljkovac remained the centre of the military activity after the war broke out in the Doboj area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm that the president of the Crisis Staff in May of 1992 of Doboj was a JNA captain called Milenko Glikoric [phoen] - let me spell that for you, G-l-i --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Milovan Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Are you able to confirm that the president of the Crisis Staff was that man who was a JNA captain?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the president of the SDA and the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just for the record, I think the party he's referring to was actually the SDS and not the SDA. Maybe that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I think that must be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SDS, yes. SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This being corrected, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And he worked closely with Stankovic from what you observed when the war broke out --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- in controlling the military resources that had been left by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you observed - is this right - trucks in 1992 taking the JNA weapons and transporting them to the barracks in Miljkovac?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Weapons and armaments, ammunition and tanks were taken to Podnovlje, which is in the direction of Modrica. And units, that is paramilitary units, that were coming in from outside were given accommodation in the barracks. They were the so-called reservists, bearded men who rampaged in the city, who provoked, sang Chetniks songs, et cetera. So they found accommodation in the 4th of July barracks as reserve units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. So from what you observed, the volunteers, paramilitary groups who came into the region reported to Stankovic who then ensured they had lodgings in the old JNA barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Lodgings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from there they would receive their orders from Stankovic. Is that something you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. In March of 1991, you were on your way to Samac, and you observed a check-point 15 kilometres from Doboj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Just remember --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- what you're saying is being taped. And they were dressed like normal soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: They were reserve units. They wore military uniforms, but it wasn't the regular army. They weren't regular units. They were reservists. All reservists had been called up to report at the barracks, but the -- the Muslims and Croats did not respond to the call-ups because the president of our recognised country said on TV that nobody should report or respond to the call-ups by the regular military, but the Serbian soldiers did -- did report, and they were handed weapons and stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. So the response to the call-up meant that irregular forces or irregular men were coming into the Doboj region, being given military uniforms and acting as reserve soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Men who could, from what you observed, be perhaps better described as paramilitaries dressed in JNA outfits. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. All reservists back then in that system, we were obliged to report and establish regular military units. So whoever puts on a military uniform is -- is then a member of a unit commanded by the regular military. We were all reservists. We had the duty to report at the barracks, and we participated in exercises, and we were under the command of professional military officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. But during the war the situation changed, and those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have problems with the transcript apparently. Could we first fix that. It seems to be a technical problem. I suggest to the parties that we slowly proceed, and if it becomes really an obstacle for further proceeding, then of course we'll stop. But often when it's fixed then we have the whole transcript again because our transcriber is still active. Please proceed, and if anyone considers that we should stop, please address the Court. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Witness, you have described what the process should be or should have been for the reservists, and what I'm suggesting happened from what you observed in Doboj was a number of reservists from different areas and groups answering the call of the SDS in Doboj and entering Doboj and acting as regular military units; is that correct? I know it's a long question.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you as a citizen and you and your fellow citizens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- "acting as regular military units" creates some confusion with me. Of course, it could be that the witness is fully aware of what you meant, but I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the answer is not clear to me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me try to clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The place where the reservists who came into Doboj -- or came from Doboj would go is to the JNA barracks in Miljkovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And they would then fall into whatever military formation was being organised by Stankovic and his JNA commanders. Is that something you observed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so. I was not in the barracks. I don't know whose command they were under, but I suppose that if he was the barracks commander, then they were under his command. I don't know. I wasn't there. I can't -- I was not in the barracks, so I was not in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you something you might know then. Just to confirm, they would receive their command from whoever was the commander at the barracks. If you don't know, you don't know. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: From what you observed, though, the source of the command was the JNA structures which exist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I do object. The witness has clearly answered that he wasn't present there, so I don't know how we could ask him how he did observe anything in this regard at the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll take the objection and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What you did observe and you can testify to is that the arming which was being conducted, arms were coming from the JNA to the SDS, the SDS were distributing them to local Serbs and reservists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Stankovic was then working alongside those reservists.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Stankovic was directly involved with the reservists. I wasn't there. I didn't know who was involved in that job from the officer staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you something different. Let me take you through your account. Can you recall giving a statement to the Doboj state security service on the 11th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Who was that? Who did I apparently give my statement to? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I just want to raise one matter. As far as I can see, we have so far received no notice from either Defence teams what kind of exhibits or even prior statements they might want to use during cross-examination. I think that was part of the guidelines from the Chamber, that we would be informed at the start of the cross-examination. And regarding the prior statement, I would suggest that it would be proper to put the statement to the witness so he can actually look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends what the questions will be, but if you want to go to the content of that statement, then you still can ask questions. It's not necessarily to be done in the way that giving the statement to the witness. I leave that in the hands of Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash, but the first objection was that you had not yet provided the Prosecution with your exhibit list to be used during cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, as my learned friend perfectly knows, we had a discussion before cross where I asked one of the Prosecution to load the statements, one of which I'm about to refer to, into the e-court. Hence I had assumed Mr. Hoffmann would understand -- but, actually, it wasn't an assumption. I said to Mr. Hoffmann that I would use it during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's getting a bit picky here. But following some of the objections we had from the other side, yes, we did talk about the prior statements; yes, we were asked to actually upload all prior statements. There was no indication whether one, all of them, or some of them would be used. So following the line of objection, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you immediately asked Mr. Jordash, "Are you going to use them?" with the same kind of curiosity as I expected earlier to be with Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Well, the indication we had was then that we should upload all of them just to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not on the playground. We in a court of law where we try to seriously deal with matters. Mr. Jordash, could you inform Mr. Hoffmann at this very moment whether you want to use more than one?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I will use the 11th of August, 1992, statement. I will use the witness's statement of the 30th of November, 2007, and I will use the transcript which arose from the trial, which the statement had been compiled for, as I indicated prior to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And next time you'll spontaneously tell Mr. Hoffmann, and if you forget about it, Mr. Hoffmann will ask you about it; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And I do see that apparently the LiveNote has been fixed. There is a possibility to reconnect, at least on my computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I ask for the witness's 11th of August, 1992, statement. The number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear a thing. My -- I don't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If no one speaks, you'll not be able to test. I'll speak again. Mr. Usher, I'll speak again, and if you do not hear anything on the B/C/S channel, then we should seek the assistance of our ... technicians, I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. USHER
utterances.text: In the background you hear some fuzz or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This reminds me of another matter. Mr. Stanisic, I do understand that you can switch on and off your microphone. Is that correct? THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you mind to switch it off when you're not speaking, because it gives some background noise, and I don't think that it interrupts your hearing us. THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] I can switch it off, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And whenever you think you would need to speak, please switch it on. We have -- THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you now -- yes, I see that apparently the witness hears the B/C/S translation by now. Therefore, Mr. Jordash, you're invited to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask, please, for the witness's 11th of August, 1992, statement. The number on the right-hand corner at the top is 03000522. And could I ask for the -- obviously the witness's statement in --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please refer to the 65 ter number or the exhibit number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just to assist on that, I think those, because they are not exhibits, they actually have no 65 ter numbers. So the only thing that is as a reference would be the ERN number, which I think my learned friend just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. There is another number on the left-hand bottom corner which is 0202. I don't know if that helps. 02027929, which is the, I think, ERN number. This is the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, would you look at the document on the left and just quickly familiarise yourself with -- with it. Do you recall giving a statement on the 11th of August, 1992, to the Doboj state security?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: This could have only be in Tesanj, not in Doboj. I was not in Doboj at the time. On the 12th of July I fled Doboj, and at that time I was living in Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's just deal with -- we'll come back to that in a moment, but I hear what you're saying, but I want to first deal with the content of the statement and see if that is a statement you recall giving at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But why --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says on the 11th of August, 1992, on the premises of the Tesanj SJB. Well, I mean, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed that. I beg your pardon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall giving this statement to the State Security Service in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you gave this statement to report what had happened to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Earlier in that year in May and June and July?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the statement you gave the public security station was to state security representatives; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who were interested in recording your complaint; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the account you gave was the best account you could recall at that point in time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was 20 days or maybe a month after I had fled. I was then treated. I fled on the 14th of July. Then I spent 20 days in hospital, and then they came to fetch me, and then I provided my statement is them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the second witness's microphone please be switched on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could you please repeat the request again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One microphone was not working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fled on the 12th of July. I was fleeing for two days, and then on the 14th of July, I ended up in hospital suffering from the consequences. Then they came to fetch me, and I was taken to provide that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at this statement. Could you have a look at paragraph one, please. Is it right that you told the interviewers that you had fled from the aggression which had started with the arrest by the Serbian Army? Perhaps the better way for me to do it is just to read the statement and ask you to confirm it. Did you say: "From the aggression against Doboj until 12th of June this year, when I was arrested by the Serbian Army, I was mostly at home"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you then say: "On the 6th of May, 1992, I was arrested by the Red Berets and taken to the Serbian SUP where I gave a statement"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that was your first reference to Red Berets, am I right, when you were interviewed at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you, going on through the statement, tell the interviewers that Faruk Ajanovic, Fehro Mujakovic, and Mustafa Alicic's brother were brought with you on that day, the day you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you tell the interviewers that the Malic brothers and the sons of Milovan Suka looted your house?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Milovan Suka, or actually his son, came and they were looking for a pistol that I had, and I had a licence to carry it. That weapon was registered -- registered with the MUP. They took it away from me. They took the pistol from me. And then from the lower ground they took my child's video games - at the time it was Commodore 64 - and some other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Will you confirm that there were locals from Doboj who were working with some of the police officers harassing civilian's such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And some of those police officers and some of those locals were working with the Serbian Army. Would you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: The locals of Serb ethnicity were either members of the reserve police or the reserve military. Some organised themselves in different ways. They were known as Predo's Wolves, White Eagles. They were independent units that operated around Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's -- let's read on. The second paragraph. Did you tell the investigators that on the 12th of June, 1992, the Serbian Army had conducted a search of the area of Orasje, Krcevine, and Carsija?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these local army men also working with these local reserve military during those searches? During those arrests?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: A group appeared, and they looked like men from Krajina, men from Banja Luka. They wore Red Berets, but none of them were locals. None of them were from Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to that in a moment, because if you look at the second paragraph, you describe the men who conducted the sweep as the Serbian Army who were conducting the sweep. There's no mention there of Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: For me, for us, all those who arrested us were the Serbian Army. Those things were not done by the Muslim army. Those things were done by the Serb army. Whether they were Red Berets or Arkan's men or somebody else, in any case they were the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you use the phrase "Serb army" to describe any military formation of a Serb ethnicity at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: At that time there was no regular Serb army in the sense that they introduced themselves as such. They all worked together. When I was in prison, I was guarded by reserve police officers, active police officers, and soldiers, and those soldiers were on the strength of the reserve army and also the Red Berets. They all acted as guards. They were all one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So from what you're saying, the Red Berets were working within other units or as a separate unit? In what way were you able to distinguish the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: The Red Berets arrived in Doboj, which means that they all came in an organised way upon somebody's invitation. Their task was to arrest, to take people from their homes, to ill-treat and beat people. They had been invited. They could not just come to Doboj without being in concert with the regular army which billeted them in the barracks and in other facilities such as old people's homes and schools. That's where they slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you gave your statement in 1992, on the 11th of August, you didn't mention the Red Berets on the 12th of June, 1992. You mentioned the Serbian Army. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: For me that was the Serb army, the Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you told us a moment ago that the Serb army was anyone in the Serb military formation. Wasn't that what your evidence was a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: I said that all formations that were there were the Serb army, starting with the Red Berets and the reserve army, the reserve police. They were all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to your statement. No mention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Stanisic, we -- we usually continue until 7.00. Is that okay with you? THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be another seven to nine minutes from now. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I can ask you to turn to -- turn to the third paragraph. And you mention here Slobodan Karadzic [sic] coming to the camp during your detention on the 12th --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just for the record again, I think the misspelling of the name has happened again. There was a reference to Slobodan Karadzic, but it should be Karagic, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, that's my pronunciation. K-a-r-a-g-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you told the - is this right - the investigator at that time that Karagic came to the camp just the once; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: He came on several occasions. He had a notebook, and he asked all of us prisoners whether we had hidden any gold or money, foreign currency mostly. He asked where those were hidden, and then he promised us that he would let us go if we told him about any hidden jewellery or money. We offered to give him our property, houses, cars, and he said no, only foreign currencies or gold. And then after that he never --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt. I was just asking quite a specific question, whether you told the investigator at that time that Karagic came to the camp only once, because that's what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. -- there appears to be a -- it's perhaps your pronunciation. If you think about a grouse which gives a better "gee" and a "G." And that creates the problem. Again, I'm not talking about Famous Grouse, but a grouse. I think that's approximately the sound you have to pronounce in order to have Karagic on the transcript rather than Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I will get used to this at some point. Karagic we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, that was actually not my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not your point. I'm sorry, Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I just think that we have to be fair in reading from the statement. And it does not say that he only came once. It says he came once, so that the witness obviously is giving the event of one of those visits of Slobodan Karagic. It is not state as is suggested that the witness at the same said he only came once. That's not on the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although it may be that that would have been -- first of all, if there is any quote from a previous statement, if there's any chance of even the quote being contested as being incomplete or inaccurate, I invite the parties to quote literally and to give the proper context, and once then a witness has answered a question in relation to that, it would be for re-examination, Mr. Hoffmann, to further clarify that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you tell the investigator, as is noted on the first line of this paragraph, that Karagic came once and asked the prisoners whether any of them wanted to ransom their heads?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you reading five lines down say, "He never came again"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what I'm reading here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's what you told the investigator.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I read here. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, the answer if -- "That's what I read here. That's what it says," is still not answer to your question. What you read there, is that what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I was speaking under the impression of the 20 days that I spent in the camp. They were insisting on the names, and I gave them what I remembered, and that's how my answers were recorded, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So the impression you had during that 20 days was that Karagic had come only once. So that's why you told the investigator he'd come only once.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did come once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, that he'd come only once. He never came again. Are those the words you used to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzovic, the issue is whether Mr. Karagic came once to the camp and never again, or is that what you intended to say, or has he been more than once in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, he did come but only once. I remember that he came once. I don't know whether he came any other time, but I know that that time when he came he had a notebook, and he was looking to purchase our heads. He was looking to exchange our lives for money or gold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, within the next two minutes we have to adjourn, so if you -- but I can imagine that you would want to put another question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just moving down the statement, did you tell the investigator, in the same paragraph, a certain Slavko who used to be a prison guard, worked as guard at the entrance to the camp where you were being held? That was the Percin Discotheque. P-e-r-c-i-n.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a retired prison guard in the Doboj prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you tell the investigator that there was occasional visits from Milan Kerkez? Formally employed at --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- the Izbor cold storage plant?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HADZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he called, he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This was a local man?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness could answer that question. He was a local man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was a local who had a job at Izbor in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the clock. If this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzovic, first of all I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, not about the testimony you've given until now and also not about the testimony still to be given tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning -- tomorrow afternoon at half past 2.00. Mr. Jordash, could I inquire as far as timing is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would fully anticipate to finish within 35, 40 minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is difficult to make that estimate because Mr. Jordash has already tackled some issues, and it all depends on Mr. Jordash's future questions, but I don't think I will need more than 45 minutes or an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then see. Mr. Stanisic, we will adjourn for the day. I'm addressing you because you're not here with us in the courtroom, but you're there through the videolink. We adjourn until tomorrow, the 1st of December, and we'll not start at quarter past 2.00 as usually, but at half past 2.00 because there is a swearing-in ceremony which may not end before quarter past 2.00. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
